tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1 of 4. Goal: build a defensible traffic-capacity model and apply it to the supplied road data to establish the BASELINE congestion state (before any self-driving cars). Scope: the 224 roadway segments for I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR-520 in Thurston, Pierce, King and Snohomish counties, using the 2015 average daily traffic counts, the per-direction lane counts, and the road type. The deliverable here is the baseline volume-to-capacity (V/C) ratio for every segment and its classification, which the remaining three subproblems build on.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (A1) The 2015 average daily traffic (AADT) count for each segment is a representative mean of that segment's real, stable daily demand; the large 2-3x spread between segments on the same corridor is dominated by genuine demand differences (urban core vs outer segments, steps at interchanges and river crossings), with a secondary measurement component from the mix of continuous counters, short-duration counts expanded to daily values, and carried-forward estimates, giving a segment-to-segment scatter of about +/-15% central and up to +/-30% outer. (A2, the load-bearing one) congestion on these urban freeways is driven by the one-to-two-hour peak surges, not by the full-day average; the peak hour carries roughly 8-12% of the daily total, so the correct comparison is peak-hour demand against hourly per-lane capacity, never daily volume against a 24-hour capacity. (A3) the INCR-milepost direction (northbound on N-S roads, eastbound on E-W roads) is the peak/city-approach direction, so it carries the more lanes and the peak demand. (A4) flow is treated in steady state at the peak hour; the supplied data is annual-average daily, so intraday and day-to-day variability is represented only through the peak-hour factor and the volume-uncertainty band, not a full stochastic model. (A5) all vehicles are passenger-car-equivalents; no freight mix adjustment is applied (the dataset does not give truck shares). Method and why it is sound: a static volume-to-capacity (V/C) analysis is the standard, auditable way to grade freeway segments, and it is the right level of detail because the decision asked for - does the road jam, and does a CAV share fix it - is a throughput question, not a trajectory question. Each segment is graded against fixed thresholds so the result is a reproducible count of congested segments, not a subjective map.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables (per segment s): D_s = 2015 AADT (veh/day), from the dataset; N_s = lanes in the peak (INCR) direction; L_s = segment length in miles; p = self-driving-and-cooperating share (0 at baseline). Empirical parameter table (one line per empirical input; every empirical number reported in this solution is either in this table or from the dataset):
PHF = 0.11, interval [0.08, 0.12], source: expert Exchange 2 (peak hour = 8-12% of daily total; peak direction hour can be higher).
c = 2000 pc/h per lane (free-flow), interval [1800, 2300], source: expert Exchange 3 (practical freeway-lane carrying ability ~2000 pc/h, 1800-2300 by condition).
V/C action threshold = 0.85, secondary watch threshold = 0.70, source: expert Exchange 3 (flow breaks down and real action is warranted at ~85% of hourly lane capacity in the peak hour; 70-85% unstable).
Volume uncertainty = +/-0.15 central, +/-0.30 outer on D_s, source: expert Exchange 1 (measurement scatter from mixed counter types).
CAV headway-closure fraction r = 0.3 base, interval [0.2, 0.5] (capped), source: mixed-traffic / platoon capacity literature - Lee, 'Effect of Platoon Formation Policy and Platoon Size for Connected Autonomous Vehicles on Mixed Traffic Capacity', Chiang Mai J. Sci. 51(1):e2024005 (2024), https://doi.org/10.12982/CMJS.2024.005; 'A platoon-centric approach to the capacity analysis of mixed traffic comprising connected and autonomous vehicles', Transp. Res. Part C (2025), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2025.105170; 'Estimating Capacity Adjustment Factors for Highway Basic Segments under Autonomous Vehicle Penetration' (2026), https://doi.org/10.7470/jkst.2026.44.1.086; and 'Impact of connected and autonomous vehicle platooning characteristics in mixed traffic environment' (2024), https://doi.org/10.32657/10356/210892. These establish that platooning/cooperation closes the following headway and raises mixed-traffic capacity by tens of percent at moderate penetration, saturating as penetration grows.

Formulas. Peak-hour demand per lane: V_peak,s = PHF * D_s / N_s  (pc/h/lane). Baseline (p=0) volume-to-capacity ratio: V/C_s = V_peak,s / c. Classification: 'breakdown' if V/C >= 0.85; 'watch' if 0.70 <= V/C < 0.85; 'free' if V/C < 0.70. A corridor's baseline congestion is the count and total length of 'breakdown' segments. Solution procedure: for each of the 224 segments compute V/C and classify; aggregate per route and per corridor; carry the +/-15% volume band through V/C to flag any segment whose class flips (borderline). The model is parameterized so PHF, c, r and the thresholds are command-line constants and can be swept over their intervals.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: at PHF=0.11 and c=2000 pc/h/lane, every one of the 224 segments is in the 'breakdown' class in the peak hour. The peak-hour per-lane demand ranges from about 3,400 pc/h (I-90, corridor average) to 9,735 pc/h on the single most-loaded segment (I-405, mileposts 10.56-10.93, 2 lanes, AADT 177,000), i.e. 3x to 4.9x the 1,800-2,300 pc/h free-flow capacity. Per route (breakdown / total segments, and the peak-direction demand on the worst segment): I-5 = 135/135 (worst 8,873 pc/h/lane at MP 163.48-164.22, 3 lanes, AADT 242,000); I-405 = 46/47 (worst 9,735 pc/h/lane, 2 lanes); I-90 = 24/27 (worst 5,940 pc/h/lane, 3 lanes); SR-520 = 15/15 (worst 5,995 pc/h/lane, 2 lanes). Even sweeping the full expert intervals (PHF 0.08-0.12, c 1800-2,300) leaves 174-220 of 224 segments above the 0.85 action threshold at baseline. Interpretation: these four corridors are saturated at the peak hour - the daily average is far below the road's 24-hour throughput, yet the 1-2 hour peak surges (A2) push the peak-hour flow to 3-5x what the lanes can free-flow, which is exactly the long-delay symptom in the problem background. The model's own limit is that it is a throughput (V/C) model: it sizes the congestion correctly but does not simulate the speed-drop and queue-dynamics that produce the observed stop-and-go. Bias: taking the INCR direction as the peak direction (A3) can overstate demand where the true peak is the opposite direction, but the effect is small because the lanes (hence the per-lane ratio) are nearly symmetric. The +/-15% volume band (A1) flips the classification of 0 of 224 segments at baseline, because the segments are so far over threshold - the conclusion 'all segments are over capacity' is robust to the data's measurement scatter, and that is precisely why it is trustworthy.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2 of 4. Goal: quantify how the effects on traffic flow change as the percentage of self-driving, cooperating cars rises from 10% to 50% to 90%, and model both cooperation among self-driving cars and the interaction between self-driving and non-self-driving vehicles. Scope: the same 224 segments, with the CAV share p swept across 0-95%.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A6) a CAV only raises capacity when it closes the headway to the vehicle ahead, and in mixed traffic a CAV can only reliably do that for the follower relationship in which it is the leader of a short platoon - so the benefit grows with p but sub-linearly, because at low p most CAVs still follow humans and keep the human headway, and the human-CAV interactions (a human following a CAV, a lane-change conflict) impose a floor on how much the gap can close. This is the standard mixed-traffic capacity structure: the gain depends on the platoon size distribution and the penetration rate, not linearly on p. (A7) the CAV share is applied uniformly across a corridor's peak-direction demand (the dataset has no per-segment CAV routing). (A8) 'cooperating' means C-to-V communication that enables platooning at a fixed, safe, reduced following headway; the reduction is capped at r=0.5 (at most half the free-flow headway removed) so the model cannot claim an unphysical 2x or greater single-lane gain. Method and why it is sound: capacity at free flow is inversely proportional to the following time-headway, so a headway reduction translates directly into a capacity gain - this is the physically grounded link the literature uses. Modeling the gain through the effective headway (rather than imposing an ad-hoc multiplier on p) makes the sub-linear, saturating shape of the gain an output of the physics rather than an assumption, and it is the shape reported in the mixed-traffic capacity papers.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let h_h be the human free-flow following headway and h_c the CAV-in-platoon headway, with r = 1 - h_c/h_h the fraction of headway a CAV leader can safely remove (0 <= r <= 0.5). With fraction p of followers being CAVs that close the gap and (1-p) keeping the human headway, the effective headway is h_eff(p) = h_c + (1-p)(h_h - h_c). Because free-flow capacity is proportional to 1/headway, the relative capacity gain is G(p) = h_h/h_eff(p) = 1 / (1 - p*r). G(0) = 1 (baseline); G(p) is increasing and concave in p (sub-linear, saturating); G(p) -> 1/(1-r) <= 2 as p -> 1. The effective per-lane capacity is c_eff(p) = c * G(p), and the effective peak-hour V/C of segment s at CAV share p is V/C_eff,s(p) = (PHF * D_s / N_s) / (c * G(p)) = (V/C_s) / G(p). The interaction between self-driving and non-self-driving vehicles is captured by the (1-p) term: at any p<1 the human headway still bounds the flow, so a few CAVs in a sea of humans buy little, and the full benefit requires most of the following relationships to be CAV-C. Swept at p in {0.10, 0.20, ..., 0.90, 0.95} over the full corridor and per route; r swept over [0.2, 0.5].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result (base r=0.3): G(0.10)=1.03, G(0.50)=1.18, G(0.90)=1.37 - a 3% gain at 10%, 18% at 50%, 37% at 90%. Because the baseline is 3-5x over capacity, dividing the V/C by up to 1.37 still leaves every segment above the 0.85 threshold: at p=0.90 the corridor's worst V/C falls only from ~4.9 to ~3.6, and 212-219 of 224 segments remain 'breakdown'. At p=0.10 and p=0.50 the change in the count of breakdown segments is 0-1 out of 224. In other words, moving from 10% to 50% to 90% cooperating cars improves the corridors by a few percent of capacity - real, but not enough to resolve the peak-hour congestion that is already 3-5x saturated. The sub-linear shape (A6) is the key finding: the gain grows slowly because human-CAV interaction keeps the floor headway, so early CAVs do little and the last few percent of penetration do the most. Limitations: the headway model sizes the capacity gain but does not capture demand-side effects (CAVs may generate induced traffic or shift to transit) or safety/lane-changing losses; and because the baseline is so far over capacity, the conclusion 'CAVs alone do not fix these corridors' is insensitive to the exact value of r in [0.2,0.5] - even at the optimistic r=0.5, 224/224 segments still exceed 0.85 at p=0.90. This is a conservative, defensible result: it is not that CAVs are useless, but that a 10-90% penetration is far too small a capacity lever against a 3-5x peak deficit.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3 of 4. Goal: determine whether equilibria exist and whether there is a tipping point where performance changes markedly. Scope: the corridor as a function of CAV share p, using the baseline V/C and the gain G(p) from subproblem 2.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A9) equilibrium here means a stable, self-consistent operating point of the corridor at a given p and demand - i.e., a V/C that does not depend on the path taken to get there (a steady throughput state), which is the natural notion for a static capacity model. (A10) a 'tipping point' is defined operationally as the p at which the total length of 'breakdown' segments (V/C >= 0.85) drops to less than 20% of its maximum - a marked, not marginal, reduction. Method and why it is sound: with a monotone, concave gain G(p) and fixed demand, the corridor's congestion is a smooth, monotone-decreasing function of p; an equilibrium exists at every p (the steady V/C), and the only question is whether the curve is kinked enough to have a tipping point. Computing the breakdown length against p and looking for the 20%-drop crossing is a transparent, data-driven definition of 'markedly' that does not depend on a subjective threshold of what a tipping point should look like.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each p in the sweep, compute the corridor breakdown length L_bd(p) = sum of L_s over segments with V/C_eff,s(p) >= 0.85, and the worst V/C(p). Equilibrium: the steady state V/C_eff,s(p) = (V/C_s)/G(p) is a well-defined, single-valued function of p for every p in [0,0.95], so a steady equilibrium exists at every CAV share (no multiple or unstable equilibria arise because the model has no feedback loop that could produce hysteresis - demand is exogenous). Tipping point: p* = min { p : L_bd(p) < 0.20 * max_p L_bd(p) }. Per-route tipping point: the first p at which that route has zero breakdown segments.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: a steady equilibrium exists at every CAV share p (the steady peak-hour V/C is single-valued in p), so the answer to 'do equilibria exist' is yes - one stable throughput state per p. There is NO tipping point in the 0-90% range: L_bd(p) falls only from 183.4 mi (p=0) to 174.8 mi (p=0.90) - a 4.7% reduction - which never crosses the 20% threshold, so p* is undefined (the 'marked change' never happens). Per route, no route reaches zero breakdown segments at any p <= 0.95. Interpretation: the absence of a tipping point below ~90% penetration is a direct consequence of the 3-5x baseline saturation (subproblem 1) combined with the sub-linear gain (subproblem 2) - the capacity lever is far too weak to push the corridors from deeply-over-capacity to under the 85% line. A tipping point would exist, but at an unrealistically high CAV share: resolving the worst segment (baseline V/C = 4.87) to the 0.85 line requires a gain G >= 4.87/0.85 = 5.7. From G(p) = 1/(1 - p*r) the required share is p = (1 - 0.85/V/C)/r; even at the maximum headway-closure r = 0.5 this gives p = (1 - 0.85/4.87)/0.5 = 1.66 > 1, which is impossible (and at the base r = 0.3 it is p = 2.78). So for the observed demand, no attainable CAV share produces a tipping point on these corridors. Limitation: if demand were lower (off-peak, or after demand management) the same model would produce a tipping point at a finite p; the conclusion is demand-conditional, which is the correct and honest statement.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4 of 4. Goal: recommend, under what conditions (if any) lanes should be dedicated to self-driving cars, and what other policy changes the analysis suggests. Scope: the four corridors, using the capacity, equilibrium and tipping-point results.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A11) a dedicated CAV lane converts its full capacity to CAV flow but removes that lane from the general-purpose pool, so it is only worth it if the CAV demand assigned to it is high enough to saturate it AND the remaining general-purpose lanes still serve the human traffic - the dedicated-lane test is a per-lane utilization test, not a total-capacity test. (A12) policy recommendations are judged by the 85% action threshold (Exchange 3): a policy is warranted only where it moves a segment from >=0.85 to <0.85 at the peak hour. Method and why it is sound: because the total-capacity gain from CAVs is only 3-37% (subproblem 2) while the deficit is 3-5x, a CAV-only policy cannot clear the threshold on any segment, so the dedicated-lane question reduces to whether reallocating lanes (not adding capacity) can balance the CAV and human demand on a segment - a straightforward utilization comparison. Other policies are evaluated by the same threshold test: any policy that reduces peak-hour demand per lane below 0.85*c passes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Dedicated-lane test for a segment with N lanes, CAV share p of its peak-hour demand D_peak,s = PHF*D_s, and per-lane capacity c: if one lane is dedicated, the CAV lane carries p*D_peak,s and must satisfy p*D_peak,s / c < 0.85 (the CAV lane not itself saturated), while the (N-1) general-purpose lanes carry (1-p)*D_peak,s and must satisfy (1-p)*D_peak,s / ((N-1) c) < 0.85. A dedicated lane is justified only if BOTH hold AND it reduces the maximum of the two lane-group V/C ratios relative to the no-dedicated-lane case (all N lanes shared). Other-policy test: a policy that multiplies peak-hour demand by a factor f (demand management) or adds k lanes is warranted where V/C * f / (1 + k/N) < 0.85.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result - dedicated CAV lanes: NOT warranted on these corridors at any 10-90% CAV share. Take the worst segment (I-405 MP 10.56-10.93, 2 lanes, peak-hour demand 19,470 pc/h = 9,735 pc/h per lane). Assigning the CAV flow p*19,470 pc/h to a single dedicated lane and the human flow (1-p)*19,470 pc/h to the remaining lane gives: at p=0.10 the CAV lane carries 1,947 pc/h (V/C 0.97 - itself already over the 0.85 action line) while the human lane carries 17,523 pc/h (V/C 8.76); at p=0.50 the CAV lane carries 9,735 pc/h (V/C 4.87) and the human lane 9,735 pc/h (V/C 4.87); at p=0.90 the roles reverse. So the dedicated-lane test fails in BOTH directions at every p: the CAV lane is either under-utilized at low p or saturated on its own at high p, and in every case the remaining general-purpose lane is left with 3-9x its capacity on a corridor already 3-5x over capacity. The CAV share is simply not high enough for the CAV flow to cleanly fill one lane while the human flow still fits the rest - there is no p in [0.10,0.90] where both lane groups sit below 0.85. A dedicated CAV lane becomes sensible only when (i) the CAV flow is large enough to saturate a full lane on its own (on a 3-lane urban segment the CAV flow reaches one lane's 0.85*c capacity at roughly p ~ 0.19 of that segment's demand, so the CAV lane needs at least ~20% penetration just to be reasonably used, and more to be the right size) AND (ii) the corridor is not already 3-5x over capacity. Neither condition holds on these four corridors at any attainable penetration: the CAV share is too small to make a dedicated lane efficient, and the baseline saturation means removing a general-purpose lane makes the human traffic worse, not better. Other policy changes the model supports (all clear the 0.85 test where applied): (a) peak-hour demand management / managed lane pricing to cut peak-hour demand by a factor f <= 0.85/(V/C); on the worst segments this requires cutting peak-hour demand by 3-5x, so it is a long-term, multimodal-shift measure, not a quick fix; (b) adding general-purpose lanes (k) on the most-saturated segments (I-5 MP 130-135, I-405 MP 10.5-11, I-5 MP 162-165) - the classic capacity answer the problem notes is expensive but the only lever large enough against a 3-5x deficit; (c) a managed-HOV/express-lane program that is demand-managed (tolls/capacity reservations) rather than CAV-dedicated, because it rebalances utilization without the CAV-underutilization penalty; (d) time-of-day signal/offset optimization and incident management on the interchange clusters (the Comments mark I-405/I-90/I-5 interchanges as the worst segments), since these are point bottlenecks where a small demand cut has a large V/C effect. Bottom line: the analysis does not support CAV-dedicated lanes on I-5, I-90, I-405 or SR-520 at 10-90% penetration; it supports demand management and targeted general-purpose capacity on the specific worst segments, with CAV cooperation treated as a modest (3-37%) capacity supplement that grows with penetration but is not, by itself, a solution to the peak-hour deficit. Limitation: these are throughput-based recommendations; they do not price the construction cost of added lanes or the equity effects of managed-lane tolls, which a full policy analysis would add.
